Is the entire answer a wordplay in which "pass the course" means "cross the river," so the student failed the course simply because the river's current prevented them from crossing it?

The phrase is a wordplay. The “student” is a very smart, attentive pupil, but “course” does not mean a class here—it means a watercourse, i.e., a river. To “pass the course” therefore means to cross the river. The student could not cross it because the current was too strong and dangerous, so they failed to “pass the course.” Their intelligence and attentiveness in class are irrelevant; the failure is simply that the river could not be crossed.

The story turns on the double meaning of “course.” The student is a genuinely smart and attentive pupil, but the “course” they could not pass is not an academic class—it is a watercourse, a river. “Pass the course” means to cross that water. They were trying to cross the river, but the current was too strong and dangerous, so they could not get across. Thus they “could not pass the course” not because of any failure of intelligence or attention in class, but because the river crossing was impossible.
